commentary.seminaVerbi:
Abram’s call and the mountain vision share one psychic move: the self is torn from tribe, then re-founded by an encounter that exceeds it. Leaving “father’s house” is the break with inherited identity; the promise is not comfort but a new center of gravity that reorganizes loyalty, memory, and future. The blessing that radiates “in thee” reads like the paradox of individuation: the more singular the vocation, the wider its human reach.

On the mountain, radiance is not ornament but disclosure: the ordinary teacher suddenly carries the unbearable weight of meaning. Moses and Elijah function like the mind’s great authorities—law and fire, structure and ecstasy—showing up to certify, then yielding. Peter’s huts are the familiar reflex to domesticate the numinous, to make a museum of the moment. The cloud and the voice cut that down: not preservation but obedience, not building but listening.

Fear and the touch belong together. Terror is the body’s truth when the ego realizes it is not sovereign; the hand and “fear not” are the re-entry into life with the experience integrated rather than fetishized. “Only Jesus” is the psychological narrowing after vision: when the scaffolding of symbols falls away, one concrete path remains.

Semina Verbi: Abram’s departure resembles the Hindu sannyasa motif—renunciation as liberation from kin-identity into a larger dharma. The transfigured figure on the mountain echoes the Buddhist sambhogakaya radiance of awakened presence, speculation, where luminosity signals a mode of being rather than a costume. The cloud-and-voice resembles the Daoist sense of the Dao that cannot be seized, only heeded, and the Zen warning against “making nests” in enlightenment—Peter’s huts as spiritual clinging. The command to keep silence until the right season parallels the esoteric discipline in Sufism and in the Eleusinian-type mystery logic: vision matures in secrecy before it can bear fruit in public.
commentary.excursus:
The call to Abram is not a tender invitation; it is an extraction. Leave country, kin, father’s house: the self is cut loose from its origins so it can be renamed and used. The promise of blessing reads like a contract with teeth—benefits, protection, retaliation—power offered in exchange for exile. “In thee” the world is blessed, but the price is that Abram becomes a conduit, not a home. Desire is drafted into history, and dread is the fuel.

On the mountain the disciples get what Abram never got: a glimpse of what this demand serves. The transfiguration is unbearable beauty, the kind that makes you want to build and stay. Peter’s tabernacles are a panic response: if we can frame it, we can keep it, we can domesticate the radiance and avoid going back down. The voice interrupts like a veto; even revelation is not for possession.

They fall facedown not from reverence but from terror at being seen through. Then the touch: not triumph, but a small human contact that breaks the spell. When they look up, the others are gone; only Jesus remains, stripped of spectacle. And the command to silence is the cruel mercy: you don’t get to turn the vision into currency. You must carry it as a wound until loss completes it.
commentary.synthesis: God elects by commanding departure and by naming the Son; salvation history is mediated through a chosen one and culminates in obedience to Christ’s voice.

gospel.text: The scene functions as a controlled disclosure to authorized witnesses: a private summit, then immediate descent, then enforced silence. Fear is not corrected by explanation but by contact and command, preparing the disciples to hold glory and suffering together without collapsing one into the other.

Moses and Elias appear as the law-and-prophets horizon, but the voice reorders authority: revelation is no longer primarily textual or prophetic mediation but filial speech. The mountaintop becomes a courtroom where the Son is publicly named and the disciples are assigned their posture: listening.

reading.text: The narrative establishes faith as migration under command: the future is located in God’s speech, not in geography or genealogy. The text makes Abram’s movement the hinge by which later election and covenantal history can exist at all.

The promises are structured to make Abram a conduit: personal elevation serves a wider economy of blessing and judgment. The universality is not generic; it is mediated, tying the fate of “kindreds” to a particular line and its God.

marginalia.text: The call is subtraction: country, kin, father—three cuts before any gift.
Promise runs through names: nation, blessing, renown. Identity is granted, not achieved.
Blessing weaponized into a boundary: alignment brings life, opposition draws curse. Universal reach is routed through a single “in thee”.
Obedience arrives without speech. Age is noted to shame excuses; Lot’s presence hints at unfinished leaving.
Light claims the body: face like sun, clothes like snow—creation’s extremes pressed into one figure.
Peter tries to freeze revelation into real estate: three booths, equalized honors, managed glory.
The cloud interrupts human plans; the imperative is not “build” but “hear.” Sonship outranks tabernacles.
After theophany, the remainder is singular: no one, only Jesus. The vision subtracts until the center remains.
Glory is embargoed until blood and rising interpret it. Timing is part of truth.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord, holy Father, you who have commanded us to listen to your beloved Son, nourish our spirit with your word; thus, with a pure gaze, we shall joyfully behold the glory of your face. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit and is God for ever and ever.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:

After Second Vespers of Sunday or of solemnities that fall on Sunday:

Humbly we ask you, Lord, that after celebrating this day the mysteries of the resurrection of your Son, we may rest in your peace without any fear, and in the morning rise with joy to sing your praises once more. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

After Vespers of solemnities that do not fall on Sunday:

Visit this room, Lord; drive far from it the snares of the enemy; let your holy angels dwell here and keep us in peace, and may your blessing remain always with us. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Compline

lines: And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and out of thy father's house, and come into the land which I shall shew thee.
And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and magnify thy name, and thou shalt be blessed.
I will bless them that bless thee, and curse them that curse thee, and IN THEE shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.
So Abram went out as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him: Abram was seventy-five years old when he went forth from Haran.
readings.heading: A reading from the Book of Genesis

lines: And after six days Jesus taketh unto him Peter and James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into a high mountain apart:
And he was transfigured before them. And his face did shine as the sun: and his garments became white as snow.
And behold there appeared to them Moses and Elias talking with him.
And Peter answering, said to Jesus: Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles, one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias.
And as he was yet speaking, behold a bright cloud overshadowed them. And lo a voice out of the cloud, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him.
And the disciples hearing fell upon their face, and were very much afraid.
And Jesus came and touched them: and said to them: Arise, and fear not.
And they lifting up their eyes, saw no one, but only Jesus.
And as they came down from the mountain, Jesus charged them, saying: Tell the vision to no man, till the Son of man be risen from the dead.
